title: Playing 3-bet pots
summary: Low SPR, the 3-bettor’s range advantage and how the caller defends.

spr.text: In a 3-bet pot the flop SPR is usually **3–5**. For example: open 2.5 BB, 3-bet to 9 BB, call. The pot is about 19.5 BB, each player has 91 BB left, SPR ≈ 4.7. At this SPR top pair with a good kicker often already plays for the whole stack.

aggressor.text: The **3-bettor** holds the range advantage: more AA, KK and AK. On ace- and king-high boards it bets often and small, **25–33% pot**. On low connected boards (7♠ 6♦ 5♣) the caller is strong too, so the 3-bettor checks more there.

caller.text:
The **caller** in position defends with floats and raises; out of position, with check-calls and check-raises. To avoid folding too often to a small c-bet, remember MDF: against a ⅓-pot bet you continue with about **75%** of your range.

The trap: in a 3-bet pot you can't "fold top pair to one bet" the way you might in a single-raised pot. The stack is small relative to the pot, and the hand strength needed to go all-in is lower.

q-spr.explain: 91 / 19.5 ≈ 4.7: a low SPR, typical of 3-bet pots.

t1.q: Who usually has the range advantage on A♠ 8♦ 3♣ in a 3-bet pot?
t1.explain: The 3-bettor holds more aces and big pairs.
